name: Chlorhexidine / antibacterial body wash
lead: Chlorhexidine is a cationic bisbiguanide antiseptic used on skin, wounds, in dentistry and on medical equipment, and it is available over the counter in the United States.[1] Chlorhexidine washes are used in healthcare for Staphylococcus aureus decolonization,[2][3] and some people use antibacterial body washes for body folliculitis.
Evidence for chlorhexidine washes comes mainly from surgical and hospital settings; no trial of its use for cosmetic body folliculitis was found.
infobox: OTC in US; some products Rx-only; WHO Essential Medicines List[1]

paras: Medical uses include pre-surgical skin and hand disinfection, wound cleaning and mouthwash; Wikipedia says 2% preparations outperform 0.5% for surgical site infection prevention, and daily chlorhexidine bathing reduced hospital-acquired infections in a US ICU trial.[1]
Reported effects include skin irritation and allergic reactions; eye contact can damage the cornea and it is ototoxic if it enters a ruptured eardrum.[1]
The positively charged molecule binds bacterial cell walls; it is bacteriostatic at low and bactericidal at high concentrations, active against many bacteria and yeasts but not spores.[1]

A trial in shoulder arthroplasty patients found neither chlorhexidine wash nor benzoyl peroxide soap effective at removing Cutibacterium from skin.[4] A study in Mohs surgery examined decolonization with intranasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine wash.[5] A review discusses povidone iodine as an alternative to mupirocin and chlorhexidine for S. aureus decolonization, citing resistance and failure concerns.[2] No studies of chlorhexidine body wash for folliculitis were found.

card.note: Can irritate skin; avoid eyes and ears per labelling.

quick.overview:
Chlorhexidine is an antiseptic widely used in surgery and hospitals, also sold as a skin wash.

Its evidence is from surgical and ICU settings; none was found for cosmetic folliculitis.
quick.mechanism: It binds bacterial cell walls and disrupts membranes.
quick.risks: Skin irritation and allergic reactions are reported; eye and ear contact can cause damage.
